utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went to PP's place, and then he recognised this rifle as being his. About the colour: When we're talking about the colour, whether the colour was brown or black, did that appear as a sticking point? Did that make him reconsider him previous statement? Was the colour a points of dispute during the second identification of the rifle?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: Sir, we talked about that, and then he made a comment, "Well, it could have been that it was painted with some shoe polish," but he was not sure about it, but he said -- made a comment -- well, he also saw some black spottings on it. And he said, "During the time, maybe the colour has been fading away," which maybe is possible. But he did not tell me that it was painted with clear paint, what -- a clear paint normally sticks for a longer time. He couldn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, why didn't you go to Witness OO, who said that it was painted and who was the first one to mention the existence of the rifle and who said that it was not the same rifle? Why didn't you go to OO? Why did you only go to PP? My question is: Why didn't you go to show the rifle to Witness OO as well as to Witness PP?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: Witness OO had stressed that it didn't have a cartridge box, it was shorter, it was certainly not this rifle, so for me there was not a reason to go to Witness OO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your mission was completed. You found the rifle. You brought it to the Prosecutor's Office. Did that bring your investigation work to an end, that is, when you came here with the Witness PP's statement and with the rifle? So did that constitute the end of your work as an investigator in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: For me, I was not directed to do any other investigations on this, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, can you remind us of the date when this rifle arrived here and when the Court was seized with the statements about the identification of this rifle. Can you remind us of the exact date when the rifle arrived and when the statements arrived.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: The rifle arrived when I came back with my mission. That must have been the 24th of January. I then -- a few days later I made my declaration, which I handed over -- I made my declaration, which was put into our system. And what -- when it was handed over to the Court, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it then when the decision was made that you would be testifying about those circumstances? Can you remember it now?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: I remember you -- you asked me if it was decided in January that I would testify about it. No, sir, because we tried to get at least Witness -- Mr. X in later, as I told you, because my colleague approached him. Then we also tried to get Mr. PP in, but he couldn't come for health reasons, and that was very recently. So it was not decided in January that I would testify. But of course I made my declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, are you aware that ever since then we have never been told that the rifle is here, that we have never been in the position to read the declaration about the identification of this rifle? Are you aware of the fact that this very important piece of evidence for the Prosecutor's Office, for which the Court ordered an investigation to be carried out, has been sitting here for months and that none of us knew anything about that? Were you the one who was guarding this rifle all this time? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: I can tell you for sure that I brought it immediately to the evidence unit and it was put there. And what happened with it later and my declaration, I cannot give you an answer on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just have a minute, please, to reorganise my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mrs. Bos, were you ever personally -- have you ever personally gone to the Bulevar, what is known as the Bulevar in the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever -- have you ever gone to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been to Santiceva Street?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever talked to a witness who told you that in Santiceva Street on the 17th of September, 1993, prisoners carried wooden rifles? From your personal experience, have you ever talked to witness who would have told you that precisely?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: I've talked to witnesses who told me about other occasions with a wooden rifle, but I cannot recall that, if that was the 17th of September, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever perhaps seen yesterday's testimony by yesterday's witness, Witness AF? You were the one who interviewed that witness, and he claimed that he had seen prisoners carry wooden rifles in Santiceva Street on the 17th of September, 1993. Do you know which witness exactly I'm talking about? He gave his testimony here before the Trial Chamber just yesterday.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: I know which witness you're talking about, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that he personally told you about having seen wooden rifles in Santiceva Street on the 17th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: I remember that, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you rule out the possibility that this wooden rifle, too, came from Santiceva Street, or can you not decide?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: I go what I've been told by Witness -- or Mr. X, who told me spontaneously about the 17th of September, who told me that he had been at the Bulevar, who told me that he had been opposite Dom Zdravlja, who also told me about other incidents he had seen there on other occasions. So for me it was clear that he was talking about the 17th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Let me get this clear. Witness X apparently also told you that he was at that moment somewhere along the Bulevar, between the medical centre and Santiceva Street. Is that what you said today?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: He said to me that he was on the very corner building at the Bulevar opposite the Dom Zdravlja. He also said to me, which is in my declaration, that there were four witnesses and one of the witnesses was heavy build and he also got cigarettes, matches, Witness PP is actually saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we've heard too. However, you also said today that Witness X told you that he had been somewhere on the Bulevar on that day, somewhere on the stretch between the medical centre and Santiceva Street. So you did say that today. I'm just wanting to make sure?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: I told you that he told me that he served quite a while along the Bulevar -- sorry, along the front line during the war. And place where is he had to serve was between the Bulevar and Santiceva Street. But on that particular day, he was on the Bulevar, opposite the Dom Zdravlja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. Bos, can we therefore agree on the following: All you really know about this rifle is what Witness X told you in relation to the rifle's origin, and that all you can tell us about the identification of that rifle is just to relate the testimony by Witness PP, who unfortunately refused to confirm his testimony before this Trial Chamber. Is that really all the information you have?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: About the wooden rifle. Yes, the information I received about it is from Mr. X and Witness PP, although I have to say that Witness PP did not refuse to come. He had serious health problems. And as I remember, in June 2001, when I contacted him to testify, a day before I contacted him in 2001, June, he had been in the hospital for check-ups also. He told me, and I was told by the AID at that time. When I contacted him again for this testifying, he agreed to testify. But then he got health problems. That's what I want to clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you insist on clarifying this point, please tell us how it came about that it was the AID who told you about his illness. Did you not contact him in person? You had to go through the AID to obtain information on his health.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: I didn't. I contacted him personally with an interpreter through the phone from The Hague to where he lives, and he told me personally that he had to go to the hospital to make an x-ray. There was no AID involved in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've referred to that just now. That's why I brought it up. Can you then please agree with me that between January last year and now we've had plenty of time to have this evidence disclosed, to wait for these potential witnesses to get better, to wait to hear you testify, to see the wooden rifle. So do you agree that between January and now this Court has not been given a chance really to discuss the problems you may have had apparently with this witness?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, that's not for me to answer this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I accept your view. Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have a number of problems here. During the break my colleague and I tried to resolve what problems we could, but only the most general points. This manufacture here, this concoction, compare it to what we had already seen, we realised that there were pages missing, that there were pages missing from this manufactured evidence. We ascertain that there were part which is didn't really correspond in the two versions but half an hour was too little time unfortunately for us to deal with this. There are, as we have realised, a number of differences that need to be studied in detail. For example, on one page you have the date "92," and the page facing this page bears the date the year of 1998. Now, all these things need to be compared. As our investigator here, today's witness, said, she did have a chance to compare the two versions -- the diary and the copy, so I would like to have a chance to question her on that. And in the typewritten pages again are different from the handwritten pages, and then those two again are different from the copies that we have in our possession. So yes, I can indeed begin my cross-examination, at least as far as the general points are concerned. But let me not take up too much time today, because tomorrow I will be able to be more focussed, because in the meantime Madam Registrar promised to have the diary scanned for me, all of it. She said she would try in as far as it was possible to do it today, so that we could have a copy before us, because I can't take this diary home, obviously, so that we could prepare really our cross-examination properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Only this, Your Honour. The Chamber will recall I think my direct examination on the diary, as opposed to the wooden rifle, took a matter of literally two or three minutes. The only things that -- the only questions I put to this witness were: When did the OTP receive the typed version? When did the OTP receive the handwritten version? When did the OTP receive the original diary through investigator Pakenham? It was carried back to The Hague. And she looked at it, and there were no obvious changes. That was the full extent of the direct examination on this witness. That's only the reason she was tendered, frankly, Your Honour, for that purpose, was to provide the Chamber a record as to when the OTP received and how we received these particular items. Now, I submit, respectfully that, Mr. Krsnik should be able to conduct his cross-examination on those four/five questions. This witness -- he can show -- he can attempt to show differences, alleged differences, to this witness all -- for weeks and we'll all still be sitting here. So we object to the anticipated scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you not object to have that document copied or scanned and furnished to the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course not. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I'm speaking on my own behalf now. If this diary has indicia of reliability, we will consider whether it should be admitted or not. We haven't made that decision yet. And obviously the "original," inverted commas, because Mr. Krsnik calls it a concoction, you present it to us as a genuine diary, the author is not here -- so as far as I'm concerned -- I've read the transcript and translation twice -- it's an important document for all people in this Court and any assistance that we can get from Mr. Krsnik, for my part, will be very readily received. May I make a suggestion in relation to one part of the diary: It was treated with ill-concealed contempt by Mr. Krsnik when it first raised its head in this Court, and if my memory serves me right, Mr. Krsnik describes it as having been written in a Serbian dialect, which no self-respecting Croat would use. Now, sure for a start we could have the translators have a look at it and assist us at least on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. I certainly agree. I point out again that this diary first -- this document, that version, to use a more neutral term, only reached The Hague on either the 26th or 27th of September. And I agree that that's perfectly fine for the translators -- one of the translators to look at that. My only question at the moment was the conclusion of the testimony of this -- this particular witness. And again, I submit, Mr. President, Judge Clark, Judge Diarra, that in any event, whatever those questions may turn out to be, they're not going to be questions for this particular witness. It came from the -- it came from Bosnia. It arrived in The Hague on the 27th of September. End of story. So whatever questions that Mr. Krsnik wants to ask somebody, I don't see why we weren't able to finish this witness's testimony today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, can't we have this one translated then, the one we've looked at today. Why is the Prosecutor saying that this is an original? What is it then that we were given if it was the 25th of September? And I know why the Prosecutor cares so much about this. They want it to be the FOSS and not the AID. But we'll clarify both of these points. But then why weren't we giving the translation? Why wasn't it disclosed to us? And who worked on this translation and who had copies made of the original? Who were those people? This is certainly no computer being used here. This is an electric-type writer. I consulted expert witnesses back in Zagreb and everybody agreed the same thing. This is an old typewriter. This is not a computer being used here to print this. This is the Ekavica not the Ijekavica dialect. In many of the document's parts. If you'll just please allow me, Your Honour, to start something. This text, purportedly part of the same original does not at all correspond with this document here. I can't say perhaps but there are many parts that don't correspond. They're not consistent, the two copies. Parts of it are different. So what translated this and who had copies made of this purported original? This is the International Criminal Tribunal and war criminals are tried here. Half an hour before I begin my cross-examination is the first time I'm actually shown the original of this document. Have had a look at it. I can't have an expert witness on it. I don't even know it exists. And I'm given something which the Prosecutor tells me is what they claim it is. And now we see there are pages missing. And this, they claim is a photocopy of the original. We don't have the whole thing. I have no right to judge on the basis of what I have here. And this is an International Criminal Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you may conduct your cross-examination to this witness tomorrow morning. And I'm afraid that you cannot get all the answers that you need, because this witness is just an investigator. She could only testify about how the OTP got this copy. As for the specific issues concerning with the language, the typewriter, as well as the style, the missing pages, I'm afraid we have to find some other experts to verify this issue. So my suggestion is -- my suggestion is you could ask any question as you like to this witness concerning with how the OTP got this diary into their possession. And then if you have some problems, other problems, you may file a motion and raise it and bring it to our attention. We'll see what we'll do concerning with this diary. Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, Your Honours, by all means. I'm perfectly clear about this. I know what the role of this witness is, and I know the extent of the testimony she can provide, and I am sure it's the same in the enemy's camp. Even today, even if she was here today just as a witness, she watched very closely, as my colleague and I were looking at this diary she remained here and she was sort of monitoring us, because that's what she was put in charge of. So my feelings were complex, because a witness who was supposed to be neutral remained -- stayed back here to monitor us, to watch us closely as we were studying the diary. We are, however, fully aware of the fact of what this investigator can give us, but I have many questions, Your Honours. I don't want it to just go by like that, because this is my last chance concerning this testimony. I'll never again have it like this. I want to question her on all the details, and I hope that Mrs. Bos will be well disposed to tell us everything she knows, like she told the Prosecution. I think it's high time this Court got familiarised with these issues relating to this diary, this alleged "diary," and these issues were issue that is our -- today's witness took part in. I have ten more minutes to go. Yes, I can take off with my cross-examination, and I promise that I will only stick to the points ordered and requested by you and to the points raised by the Prosecutor's Office. But I will certainly request and challenge the credibility not of the witness personally but the credibility of this entire thing, the AID-related issues. I think today's witness must know this very well, because she's been working with these people for seven years. So I can start now, if you'd like me to. We have ten more minutes to go. The only thing I want to know is when I will be given copies of this alleged diary as well as the translation, if that's what it takes, of the original copy, so I can start work on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we get too far further afield -- and I would have welcomed to finish this witness today and believe that we should have on a proper scope of examination. We should have and could have -- I want to point out though a couple of items that is I think in light of what Mr. Krsnik said. On the 3rd of October, last week, it was provided to counsel, Apolonia Bos will give evidence concerning the rifle, of how the Prosecutor came into possession of the rifle, and the original -- I emphasise the word, "the original" -- Rados diary, which will be presented in Court. Estimated time of direct examination, one hour. In fact, I did it in 34 minutes. Now, since October 3rd, there was never a request from the Defence to inspect the diary, never a call, never a telephone call, never coming across the courtroom, never a request to examine the diary, and I submit to you, Mr. President, that's more because Mr. Krsnik would rather complain about it than in fact have access to it. That's one point. The second point is this: On the 19th of September - on the 19th of September - the entire statements of Mr. Idrizovic were turned over. Counsel has had that for some weeks. In that, counsel will know, if he's read them that, it's Mr. Idrizovic, not this witness, who will talk about finding the diary in Doljani, in July 1993, and how that witness provided it to AID later sometime in 1996 or 1997, and that witness will be shown the original -- the blue-ink diary that I've shown to the Chamber today and Mr. Idrizovic will say that is the same diary I saw in 1993. Now, that for Mr. Idrizovic to say, not for Ms. Bos to say. It came to The Hague on the 27th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, you must request private session. It's for your sake, I'm saying this, because you have disclosed a number of name, because he's a protected witness. So we should have this redacted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, he's not. Mr. Idrizovic wants to testify publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Finally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that we don't have time for you cross-examination this afternoon, so you may continue your cross-examination tomorrow morning. But Mr. Krsnik, this Trial Chamber has already informed you that you cannot get all the answers from this witness tomorrow. So I believe that your cross-examination will be limited to the area how the OTP got in the possession of this diary. You have other opportunities to rebuttal everything. You could file a motion concerning all those language issues, the typing issues, as well as others in your motion. You could call your witnesses in rebuttal, and there is another witness who will testify about this diary in the rebuttal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So tomorrow morning I believe you have 30 minutes to conduct your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honours, I need more than that, and I'd like to tell you that immediately I do have the right to question the credibility and the circumstances surrounding this credibility. The Prosecution's case questioning was three to four times longer than ours, and I'm telling you right now I can't have only 30 minutes, because that's not enough time and please apply the same yardstick as you did to the Prosecution case. I know that we are again severely prejudiced in this here because we are the ones cutting our own time short. We have the adjoinder on Monday. How much time shall we have left to draft our final brief? This is only prejudicial to us, the Defence team. We are aware of that. We are perfectly aware of that. But we want to finish this cross-examination and conduct it in the proper way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you know the Prosecution used time in the direction examination for 5 or 6 minutes. I'll give you 30 minutes, it's 5 times more than the time spent by that of the Prosecution. You have to organise your cross-examination in a good way tonight, and I will guarantee you that a copy of that diary will be furnished you before 5.30 today. We will rise until 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
